newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says Natuna gas field work on track.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says Natuna gas field work on track.

text.p: Indonesia's national oil company Pertamina has brushed off reports that its giant Natuna gas project has been mothballed following a big gas find elsewhere in the archipelago, stressing that it is on track to commence production.
Newspapers have said the Natuna project in the South China Sea has been put on ice following a gas find by Atlantic Richfield Co (Arco) of the United States in Indonesia's Irian Jaya province.

"It is totally untrue. Natuna will continue to develop. We expect to make first deliveries in the year 2002 from Natuna," G.A.S. Nayoan, a senior Pertamina executive involved in the Natuna project, told Reuters on Friday.
He said a continuing cost-cutting programme in the Natuna project would market the gas at competitive prices.
Nayoan said the offshore Natuna project would have 16 platforms instead of 18 planned originally to produce 2.4 billion cubic feet of gas a day.
He said 216 wells for production and 84 wells for reinjecting waste gas would be drilled around the Natunas, a string of islands about 1,100 km (680 miles) north of Jakarta.
"Tender notifications in national newspapers have already begun. For example, in April this year a notification was given to tender for the conceptual engineering contract," he said.
"In October a tender for air transport was also notified."
He said the involvement of giant oil companies -- Exxon Corp and Mobil Corp -- would guarantee efficiency and lead to competitive prices.
Exxon has a 50 percent stake in the Natuna project, Mobil 26 percent and Pertamina 24 percent.

"There is no conflict between the Arco gas find in Wiriagar, Irian Jaya and the Natuna gas project. We are thankful for that (Arco) find. But the Arco gas finding has not been certified. We still not know how much exactly the gas reserves there are," Pertamina's general affairs director Baharuddin told Reuters.
Arco said on June 18 that five drill-stem tests of the Wiriagar Deep-3 appraisal well in Irian Jaya province achieved a cumulative natural gas rate of 43 million cubic ft per day.
It was the fourth well in a multiple-well appraisal programme on the Berau block of Bituni Bay, Irian Jaya, the western half of New Guinea island.

Pertamina and Exxon signed an agreement in 1994 to exploit the Natuna field, which contains an estimated 210 trillion cubic feet (tcf) of gas, of which 45 tcf are thought to be recoverable commercially.
Pertamina's exploration director Priyambodo Mulyosudirdjo said the company was committed to develop and utilise any resources found.

"It is our duty to develop and to utilise all resources that we find. As we know, the main problem for the gas is how to find the market. But we are hopeful that we can do so," Mulyosudirdjo told Reuters.
Baharuddin said gas from Natuna was ready to be marketed because 29 tcf of gas reserves had been certified and the technology to exploit it was available.
"At the moment Natuna gas is ready to be marketed, because we already know the reserves and the technology. We are offering a 30-year (supply) contract from Natuna," he said.
"Beside seeking to pipe the gas, we also plan to build a liquefied natural gas plant there," Baharuddin said.
He said talks to pipe the gas to Thailand from Natuna were still in progress. Pertamina had also offered the gas to South Korea and Japan.
